title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
body: I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem. title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
body: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. README 節錄：# print-my-profile-pic Star this repo to have your GitHub profile picture framed, printed out on my receipt printer, and stuck to my wall. That's it! > [!TIP] > If you give a one-time sponsorship of any amount beforehand, your profile picture will be printed in a **special frame**. ## How's it work? GitHub allows you to create webhooks for specific events on your repos, I've set one up for starring this project. When that happens, a payload is POSTed to a Cloudflare tunnel domain, which leads to a PHP script running on a Raspberry Pi that's sitting on my desk. From the inbound request, you can gleen info about the person who starred the repo, like their display name and avatar URL. The script takes their profile picture, renders it behind a cut-out of a photo frame, and then adds some other info I thought should be included in each receipt. The RPi is connected to an Epson TM-T88IV thermal receipt printer via USB, and the PHP script uses my go-to escpos-php library to format the receipt data and send it off to the printer. ## But why? README 節錄：# florilegium ## Origin The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original. This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life. ## What it is Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden. Try it in your browser. The playground sets a page as a printer's proof, grows its margin with the same Lua, and hands it back as an SVG, a LaTeX preamble or a Typst page setup. *Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.* Two documents share one package, and two more (`showcase.tex`, `spread.tex`) show what else it does: | | `florilegium.tex` | `florilegium-grow.tex` | |---|---|---| | composition | **authored**: stems, leaves and flowers
